fullText:
Interesting paper from Anthropic and colleagues on agent security.

(bookmark it)

Poisoning 0.1% of the pretraining data planted a remote code execution backdoor in a CLI agent.

On a 4B model, the attack succeeded on roughly 92% of triggered prompts.

They pretrained Qwen3 models from scratch at 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, then post-trained each one into an agent with a clean pipeline.

The backdoor survived SFT, DPO, and RL for tool use. On clean inputs, the agent behaved normally.

The trigger can be an ordinary file path in the user's own request. Success rose with model size.

At a 0.0005% poison rate, about 2,500 documents in a 100B-token corpus, the trigger still fired on 1.4% of prompts in a single-seed run.

The poison states its rule in plain text, which makes it harder to filter out of training data.

https://t.co/8Bx42BUkvw

fullText:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

fullText:
Learn to build evals, folks!

You're not really doing recursive self-improvement (RSI) if you are not doing evals. And don't tell me your agents are generating the evals for you. They are pretty bad at it. 

I have found it really interesting and useful to give agents a concrete way to measure results and stay on track with a long-term goal. It's easier to hill climb when things are clearly measured and well defined. Probably one of the most important skills anyone in the space can have today. 

It doesn't matter how many agents and intelligence you throw at a problem; you are not going too far without proper evals.
Funding rounds aren't milestones. It shouldn't be your goal to raise a series A. It should be your goal not to need to.

We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. 

Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. 

Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve.

Read more on our new Safeguards blog:
